item.title: The Witcher 3 Remastered Makes Even the Best Open-World RPGs Feel Dead
item.description:
I've been enjoying another tumultuous playthrough on The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered , and I'm especially enjoying revisiting the gorgeous views and bustling cities of the Continent. The upgraded graphics make Geralt's journey exceptionally alluring, and between each familiar location and unexpected encounter, it made me think of how vibrant The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt 's world feels. While plenty of other medieval-inspired open-world RPGs also offer gorgeous landscapes and fascinating lore, they don't always capture that same sense of living, breathing spirit that I experience when on the Continent.

I have played most of the medieval-inspired RPGs out there, but something about The Witcher 3 stands out to me: the folklore, fairytales and village culture feel so embedded in each quest, as well as the moving world around it. I feel like it retains that Middle-Age, 13th-Century imagination with its rural superstition, herbal remedies, and fear of the supernatural. Many of the monsters that players meet on Geralt's journeys are directly inspired by real folklore creatures, and I think that the game does exceptionally well to express this through its varied villages, castles, and cities, which each have their own fable to tell.

The Witcher 3 Remastered Mods Prove Why Skyrim Still Matters

The Witcher 3 Remastered's mod scene is growing fast, and Skyrim is still the clearest example of how much that can matter years later.

By Jane Vincent

The Witcher 3 Villages Make the Continent Feel Alive With Folklore and Monsters

Though I mostly like to spend my time within the thriving walls of Novigrad, I also enjoy visiting each of the villages on my way to whatever quest or contract Geralt has been sent on, and each excursion itself is ripe with monsters and other creatures. For most, the first that Geralt confronts is The Beast of White Orchard , otherwise known as a Griffin which he and Vesimir attempt to lure to the grassy plains with the ill-smelling buckthorn. The Beast of White Orchard quest itself feels like the first chapter of the many tales that Geralt goes on to discover, especially when learning that the Griffin has been terrorizing the region for a while. This immerses players directly into the story of The Wild Hunt , where it feels like trouble is brewing, regardless if Geralt is there to aid or not.

Tier List

Available Options

Add To Tier

There is plenty of folklore across the rest of the Continent too, and each location has its own vibrant network of characters. In Velen, there's Blackbough, with its woodland monsters, and Downwarren, home to the Crones of Crookback Bog, who are themselves surrounded by Drowners and Water Hags. The Family Matters quest itself has its own savage mystique, and in Crow's Perch you meet the Bloody Baron, whose family conflict lies at the heart of his stronghold's personality. Players see firsthand how the Bloody Baron's temper affects his fortress, keep, and those who live in it. The countless missing posters of his wife, Anna, and daughter, Tamara, only add another shade of mystery to Geralt's exploration of the region.

Every Region in The Witcher 3 Has Its Own Unique Identity

Velen isn't the only region which is abundant with personality, and I want to focus now on the network in these locations. In Skellige, there's Kannvaig, which is a seafaring, Scandinavian-inspired village. Kannvaig has its own folklore, tradition, and set of coastal monsters. Even its architecture contributes to Skellige's rugged, maritime, atmosphere, and I think that it's this sense of eccentricity that makes The Witcher 3 's world so animated. In the Blood and Wine expansion's Toussaint, there's Dun Tynne, a castle which reminds me of the aristocratic, fortified noble residences of Medieval times, especially with its chivalrous knights and picturesque countryside. Coronota Vineyard is full of its own wine culture, and Geralt helps solve problems and infestations of the estate in the Wine Wars quest line. So, each settlement in The Witcher 3 has its own individual particularity, which is often even distinguished by the slight lilt of the regional accent.

If you haven't come across Toussaint in your playthroughs, that's because it's exclusive to The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt 's Blood and Wine expansion, which must be purchased separately from the base game unless included in a bundle or edition you own. The expansion introduces Geralt to an entirely new region, complete with its own main storyline, characters, quests, and locations, including Beauclair and the surrounding vineyards.

It's important that The Witcher 3 's smaller areas hold this distinctive energy, because each of them contributes to the Continent's liveliness. I don't see this level of spirit in every medieval-inspired RPG: in The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim , though most of the towns and cities have a clear faction or allegiance, the constitution feels more or less the same. Don't get me wrong, I think that Tamriel is dynamic in its own right, but I don't get the same sense of foreboding or mystery as I do when playing The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt . Even the dungeons you explore are more or less the same in their look and feel.

In Elden Ring , the Lands Between are deliberately ruined, with few ordinary people living together in "functioning" communities. The game prioritizes decay and isolation over bustling village life, but it's clear that The Witcher 3 connects the threats of monsters and folklore-inspired creatures to the everyday lives and beliefs of local people. And though Dragon's Dogma 2 does have impressive monster encounters and a beautiful fantasy landscape, its comparatively shallow towns and NPC interactions limit the personality of certain settlements.

The Witcher 3's Folklore Is About Understanding Monsters, Not Just Hunting Them

To me, folklore is the living belief system in The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt. The villagers don't just coexist with the surrounding monsters, and their rituals and fear of the supernatural influence how they behave and make decisions. This isn't just limited to the dangerous, though. During a recent playthrough of Novigrad Dreaming, I investigated the haunted house as Geralt aimed to help Corinne Tilly, a dreamer. After discovering Sarah, the Godling, and making a few more choices, the section ended, and I moved on to the next phase of the quest line. However, a while later, I decided to revisit Corinne and Sarah. I was rewarded with a short cutscene and the Haunted House secondary quest, which I hadn't encountered in my previous playthrough.

It was that cutscene that stood out to me, though, because of its black-and-white, storybook-like animation that is usually at the start of each load. The cutscene retells Corinne, Sarah and Geralt's story in a dramatic but important way: it plays with folklore's tendency to cast strange beings as dangerous. To me, it felt like understanding Sarah's motives changed the story entirely. It's the little moments like this where The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt showcases such a richly embedded, and surprisingly grounded, depiction of medieval-inspired folklore. It invites the players to contradict and even rewrite these tales, rather than letting them pass by unmoved.

The Witcher 3 Remains the Gold Standard for a Living, Breathing Fantasy World

I've yet to find a world as captivating as I've experienced in The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt , and the Remastered version is letting me experience its allure all over again. After deliberating on why the world feels so effortlessly alive, I've given the folklore strong credit. There are plenty of other reasons that add to the Continent's dynamic, though, such as Gwent, the functioning trade network and environmental storytelling. I also think that the choices Geralt makes change how players interpret folklore, like with Sarah the Godling: Geralt must ultimately investigate local beliefs rather than automatically accept them.

The Witcher 3 Remastered Just Broke a Steam Record, and RPG Remasters Should Take Notes
The Witcher 3 Remastered Mods Prove Why Skyrim Still Matters
Witcher 3 Remastered Actually Makes Old Saves Better Than New Game Plus

This is not to make the point that The Witcher 3 has more lore than every other medieval-inspired RPG: that would be a much harder claim to make. But I really do think that it's how lore matters to the people living in the world. Other RPGs excel at world-building in their own ways, but The Witcher 3 remains an extraordinary example of how to make a fantasy world feel lived in, and I'm looking forward to seeing the next medieval-inspired open-world RPG to bring that same level of energy into their world (and frankly, I think that Fable has a great chance).

The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Remastered

Monopoly GO Station Sprint Rewards Overview

Station Sprint has 100 milestones, with a total of 112,900 points required to claim every reward. Although reaching the end of the track is going to take a huge number of dice rolls, ou can still collect plenty of useful items without completing every milestone.

Here's a quick look at the main rewards available throughout Station Sprint:

  • 25,900 free dice rolls across the full milestone track.
  • 8,650 Flags for the K-pop Demon Hunters Racers event.
  • 5,000 dice rolls at Milestones 62 and 100.
  • 2,200 dice rolls at Milestone 56.
  • 1,650 dice rolls at Milestone 48.
  • 1,400 dice rolls at Milestone 43.
  • 1,100 dice rolls at Milestone 35.
  • 925 dice rolls at Milestones 25 and 39.

The Flags are a must-grab, especially while K-pop Demon Hunters Racers is active. You can collect them through Station Sprint and use them to participate in the racing event, where you can win extra dice rolls and sticker rewards. You don't necessarily have to finish all 100 milestones to build up a useful supply.

Best Strategy for the Monopoly GO Station Sprint Event

Station Sprint is a Pickup event, so your points come from landing on tiles marked with the event's special Pickup icon . Each successful landing awards 2 points x your current dice multiplier.

As always, keep an eye out for several Pickup tiles grouped close together. If you have a reasonable chance of landing on one of them, a higher dice multiplier can help you earn more points from a successful roll.

Try to reach around Milestone 31 if you want a more manageable target. By then, you'll have earned approximately 1,380 Flags. This can be a useful stopping point if you'd rather save your dice than push through the more expensive later stages.

Avoid using your highest dice multiplier on every roll. Save it for situations where multiple Pickup tokens are within a reasonable reach, and reduce it when the board offers fewer useful landing opportunities.

If you're running low on dice, collect any available free Shop gifts and complete Quick Wins. While K-pop Demon Hunters Racers remains active, these are additional ways to gather Flags alongside the rewards from Station Sprint and Spooky Express.

Monopoly GO Station Sprint FAQs

When does Station Sprint end in Monopoly GO?

Station Sprint starts on October 16, 2026, at 1 PM ET and ends on October 18, 2026, at 4 PM ET. You have just over two days to work through its 100 milestones.

How many dice rolls can you earn in Station Sprint?

You can earn a total of 25,900 free dice rolls by completing all 100 milestones. The largest individual dice rewards are 5,000 rolls at Milestones 62 and 100.

How many Flags can you get from Station Sprint?

There are 8,650 Flags available across the full milestone track. These can be used in the K-pop Demon Hunters Racers event.

Try to reach around Milestone 31 if you want a more manageable target. By then, you'll have earned approximately 1,380 Flags. This can be a useful stopping point if you'd rather save your dice than push through the more expensive later stages.

Avoid using your highest dice multiplier on every roll. Save it for situations where multiple Pickup tokens are within a reasonable reach, and reduce it when the board offers fewer useful landing opportunities.

If you're running low on dice, collect any available free Shop gifts and complete Quick Wins. While K-pop Demon Hunters Racers remains active, these are additional ways to gather Flags alongside the rewards from Station Sprint and Spooky Express.

Monopoly GO Station Sprint FAQs

When does Station Sprint end in Monopoly GO?

Station Sprint starts on October 16, 2026, at 1 PM ET and ends on October 18, 2026, at 4 PM ET. You have just over two days to work through its 100 milestones.

How many dice rolls can you earn in Station Sprint?

You can earn a total of 25,900 free dice rolls by completing all 100 milestones. The largest individual dice rewards are 5,000 rolls at Milestones 62 and 100.

How many Flags can you get from Station Sprint?

There are 8,650 Flags available across the full milestone track. These can be used in the K-pop Demon Hunters Racers event.

item.title: New Retro Survival Horror Game on Steam Is Like PS1 Resident Evil, and It's Seriously Impressive
item.description:
Call me late to the party or what have you, but growing up, I was mostly a Nintendo kid with some Sega on the side. Almost every console I owned was a Nintendo console, and while I don't regret it at all, I do wish I hadn't missed out on the early PlayStation days. Sure, I got to occasionally play some classic PS games at Sears— Crash Bandicoot being the one I remember the most—but it wasn't until the release of Final Fantasy 10 on the PS2 that I finally became a part of the PlayStation family. Since then, I have purchased every generation of PlayStation console, especially as its exclusives have become increasingly sought after. Well, despite the fact that I've been in on PlayStation since the PS2, that still means I missed out on the platform's earliest classics, including the original Resident Evil . Now, after playing the Overwhelmingly Positive demo for Phase Zero on Steam , I witnessed firsthand what I missed out on, and I'm seriously impressed by it.

Something else that makes Phase Zero such an interesting case for me personally is that I wasn't always a fan of horror either. I was one of those teenagers who was scared by the Flood in the original Halo . Of course, I knew I wasn't alone there, but it nonetheless didn't take much to give me a fright. Now, though, I love the thrill that horror franchises like Resident Evil give me, especially when they're coupled with survival elements that keep me on my toes. That's precisely what SPINA Studio's Phase Zero brings to the table, with its Steam page even explicitly describing it as featuring "pre-rendered backgrounds, fixed cameras and the DNA of the PSX masterpieces," blending "nostalgic design with modern quality-of-life improvements, while honoring its iconic roots."

The Walking Dead Meets Resident Evil in Chandler Riggs' New Fan Film

Two of the biggest zombie franchises of all time, The Walking Dead and Resident Evil, are finally crossing paths, thanks to Chandler Riggs.

By Charming Holiday

Phase Zero Perfectly Encapsulates the PS1-Era of Resident Evil

Check Out Phase Zero's Overwhelmingly Positive Demo on Steam

Phase Zero takes place in 1994 in Flint Peak, a remote harbor town that's already having a rough time before the player even sets foot in it. A brutal snowstorm is on the way, but that's the least of the town's worries, as a mysterious illness has been spreading through the area and turning its residents into some pretty horrifying creatures. Rather than following just one character through the whole ordeal, Phase Zero tells its story across multiple chapters from the perspectives of different survivors, each trying to make it through the night with whatever supplies they can find. Of course, simply surviving isn't the only thing they're concerned about, as there's also the mystery of what's causing the outbreak in the first place.

Wishlist Today

The demo for Phase Zero only features one playable protagonist, and I was able to reach the end of the preview in around half an hour. However, even with the demo being such a small slice of what Phase Zero 's full release will bring when it launches on March 11, 2027 , it certainly didn't feel like a small slice. Rather, not only did I feel like I was able to get a firm grasp on what Phase Zero was trying to do in my short time with the game, I was honestly blown away by the fact that what initially seemed like such an unassuming indie game turned out to offer me an unforgettable, meaty experience right out of the gate. I can confidently say that just 30 minutes with Phase Zero was enough to make me want so much more of this world that SPINA Studio has put together, retro feel and all.

Granted, I did have to change the controls to "modern" pretty much right away, as I just couldn't get used to the classic control scheme. That essentially meant putting the control stick in charge of all movement, rather than the D-pad, which it defaulted to. The fixed camera, on the other hand, is something that I really appreciated, especially considering Final Fantasy 10 was the first PlayStation game I ever owned, and it also featured a fixed camera. It was just the right amount of nostalgia without making the whole experience too complicated to navigate.

Phase Zero 's Steam demo currently has an Overwhelmingly Positive rating.

But nostalgic touches aside, the experience that Phase Zero offers is immensely unforgettable. Atmosphere is everything in a survival horror game, and that is one area Phase Zero absolutely excels in. To me, that just proves you don't need great visuals or high-fidelity audio design to sell immersion and atmosphere. Instead, you can do it through setting and silence—two elements Phase Zero expertly establishes from the get-go.

The demo had its playable protagonist, Guy, waking up in a Flint Peak hospital just as a mysterious outbreak begins turning the town's residents into zombies. Maybe it's a bit of a Walking Dead -type setup, but it's effective at establishing panic and urgency immediately. From there, you're left to figure things out alongside Guy, who quickly decides the nearby window is his only escape route but has no idea of where to go or what to do next.

Phase Zero's Resident Evil Inspiration Goes Deeper Than Its Looks

And just as Resident Evil games have always done, Phase Zero sells its tension even further with its survival elements, including limited ammo and health kits, as well as no idea of what to do next. At the same time, the demo is somewhat forgiving if you've played these games before and understand that you can't afford to fire every bullet you've got. Some encounters just need to be evaded or escaped once a grapple begins. And speaking of grapples, if a zombie grabs you, you can get out of its hold and kill it in the process, but just like in Resident Evil , it costs you a bit of health to do so.

Exploration in Phase Zero is already proving to be satisfying as well, with the same "find a way forward" loop survival horror games like Resident Evil have always implemented. There's plenty of lore to be found while exploring, with each note you pick up or picture you look at giving more details about the outbreak, but what's so satisfying is how the world itself tells the story. Each step forward offers up more details about what went wrong simply because the environment says so, and that's also where it gets increasingly immersive. And many of those steps forward are initially blocked by a puzzle that needs solving, making progression all the more rewarding when it happens.

I can confidently say that just 30 minutes with Phase Zero was enough to make me want so much more of this world that SPINA Studio has put together, retro feel and all.

But I do need to mention the voice acting, because it's actually very good. The characters' lips don't move, of course, as this is intentionally designed to reflect the PS1 era of character design. However, the voices that come out of these characters are, I'd say, more convincing than some AAA games. I'm not suggesting that voice acting is everything in a game, but when there's a story being told, bad acting can really pull you out of it. That doesn't happen in Phase Zero , at least during what I played in the game's demo.

I think what excites me most about Phase Zero now is getting to see more of Flint Peak and finding out just how far SPINA Studio is willing to take this experience. After all, the demo only gave me a glimpse of the town and its story, and if the rest of the game is anywhere near as immersive as what I played, I can already see myself getting lost in it for hours. I'm especially looking forward to seeing how the mystery unfolds, because even in the short time I spent with the game, I found myself paying attention to just about everything around me, wondering whether the next room or document I came across might have something important to tell me. And I love that. It's one thing for a survival horror game to make me afraid of what's around the corner, but it's another thing entirely to make me genuinely curious about what's there.

New Retro Survival Horror Game on Steam Is Like PS1 Resident Evil, and It's Seriously Impressive
The Walking Dead Meets Resident Evil in Chandler Riggs' New Fan Film
Resident Evil Requiem Proves Veronica Needs More Than New Controls
Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil: Wētā FX Breaks Down the Pedestrian and More - Interview

Ultimately, I think Phase Zero has already accomplished exactly what it set out to do, at least as far as I'm concerned. I may not have grown up playing the original Resident Evil games, but I certainly understand their appeal a lot better now, and I love that SPINA Studio is bringing that style of survival horror back for both longtime fans and people like me who missed out on it the first time around. Of course, I'll have to see how the full game turns out when it launches on March 11, 2027, but for now, I'm just glad I decided to give its demo a shot. Phase Zero wasn't even on my radar before I played it, and now it's easily one of the indie games I'm most looking forward to playing next year. And considering it only took about 30 minutes to get me there, I'd say that's pretty impressive.

Phase Zero launches on Steam on March 11, 2027. A free demo is currently available, and the full game can be wishlisted.

item.title: Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Gives First Official Look at Dark Link
item.description:
A new trailer has been released for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Nintendo Switch 2, offering a first look at the fight with Dark Link. There are many reasons that Zelda: Ocarina of Time is so well regarded, and part of it can be attributed to the game's memorable boss fights. Link's quest to save Hyrule pits him against enemies like King Dodongo, Twinrova, and Ganondorf himself. Nearly three decades after the game's release on N64, those boss fights remain iconic.

In many ways, it seems the Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake will be faithful to the game that was released on N64. The story beats clearly remain the same, though fans of the N64 game should still expect to see some changes. Voice acting and majorly overhauled visuals are present, and Zelda: Ocarina of Time has a new Hall of Fallen Foes. The area will allow players to see the enemies they defeat in the game, and present the opportunity for rematches.

Nostalgic Zelda: Ocarina of Time Midnight Launch Bonus Officially Revealed

Retailers are having midnight openings for the Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, and one is offering a nostalgic bonus for N64 fans.

By Marc Deschamps

New Ocarina of Time Trailer Reveals Dark Link

As part of the ramp up to Zelda: Ocarina of Time 's November 5 release date, a new video was released on Nintendo UK's YouTube channel. The video offers a glimpse at several sequences that might be familiar to those who played the original game, though it showcases how they've been changed on Nintendo Switch 2. The video starts with Ganondorf playing the piano before jumping into a series of clips showing Link battling with some major enemies. One of those enemies happens to be Dark Link, a foe players come across in the infamous Water Temple.

item.title: Red Dead Redemption 2 Has One Bad Habit GTA 6 Must Finally Break
item.description:
Red Dead Redemption 2 was released in 2018, almost 8 years ago, and it is still fondly talked about in the world of gaming. It's thanks to the exceptional story and characters that Red Dead Redemption 2 has the longevity that it does. Rockstar Games created a generational narrative with just about anything a person could want from a good story, from love and longing to murder and governmental interference. Characters are tangible beings with wants and desires that manifest in actions, whether good or evil, that change the course of the story. That impeccable writing is what keeps me coming back to RDR2 again and again.

Sure, I have a ton of games on my list that I need to play, but I also want to keep riding and bonding with my horse, talking to members of the Van der Linde gang, and chatting with wonderful and weird NPCs in RDR2 . Story mode is a joy to run through again and again, but the story missions can sometimes stunt exploration for players, playing out scenarios strictly without the player's control. These story missions inadvertently set invisible boundaries that keep players from inhabiting the world Rockstar built to its fullest. With strict boundaries in mind, how are players meant to get the most out of the thoughtfully crafted world and story?

Red Dead Redemption 2: Mission List

Players can find all missions and their order from Chapter to Chapter for Red Dead Redemption 2 below, without any spoilers.

1
By Jake Fillery

Story Mode Missions Set Invisible Boundaries Around What Is Supposed to Be an Open World

Rockstar managed to create an exceedingly memorable world in Red Dead Redemption 2 , crafting in-depth narratives with tangible characters that make players feel something long after they've put the controller down. The game truly has it all. High-stakes gunfights that get players' palms sweating, days-long adventures through scenic flatlands and snowy mountains to catch legendary animals, and extraordinary characters with purpose and human motives for success, a better life, or grand plans for greener pastures. Exploration is what makes Red Dead Redemption 2 worthwhile. It is the backbone of the game. Developers purposefully made the title detailed for voracious explorers to explore, down to NPC interactions and subtle environmental details that one can find that accidentally unravel a larger narrative.

Who’s That Character?

Identify the silhouettes before time runs out.

Embarking on Story Mode, players are thrust into this wide-open world, still wet behind the ears as they explore as Arthur Morgan on a mission to get the gang to safety. What transpires is a whirlwind that takes hours upon hours to get through from start to finish. From Arthur's beginnings in the snowy mountains to his end staring off at the sunrise, it took me around 62 hours to get through my first playthrough. Like many who first played RDR2 , I was eager to explore all the world had to offer, which is why it took me so long to finish the main narrative.

Rockstar managed to create an exceedingly memorable world in Red Dead Redemption 2 , crafting in-depth narratives with tangible characters that make players feel something long after they've put the controller down.

Story missions effectively halted my exploration, serving as an invisible roadblock that would require me to perform exact sequences of actions in order to understand a plot point or gain more clarity on the Van der Linde gang's situation. While I am in love with the story and what Rockstar has managed to create, I was frustrated that I had to follow guidelines to get through story missions. It seemed counterintuitive, given that once players are let loose in RDR2 , they can pretty much play however they like. There is no expectation beyond story mode. Folks can ride on horseback for hours on end, hunt massive albino alligators, or track down serial killers leaving a bloody trail on the home front.

It is an odd disconnect that one must carry out story mode missions to a T, unless they'd rather fail. These missions are made to convey a plot point in a uniform manner, but restricting characters' abilities to do and act how they please in a massive world like RDR2 's is not what many players signed up for. Why can't players be treated to a wonderful story with rich writing and dialogue, while also being able to roam as they please? It is like putting a starving person before a massive spread, but only allowing them to dig into the meat and potatoes and not the sides. Players may miss what RDR2 's world has to offer, forced to focus on a narrative fed to them in a sterilized, structured way.

My first playthrough was strictly about finding out how this story unravels, which meant I missed out on a ton. I felt roped into the story, which is a credit to the writers at Rockstar, but I also had no chance to catch my breath and just be. When I did carry out exploration, I felt free and happy, riding my horse, whom I named Whinney, and chatting with strange and wonderful NPCs who would give me quests like bone collecting or picture taking. I became someone else as I explored, eager to learn about the world around me, to get a better sense of a time I had never been a part of: the Old West.

How cool would it be to be a cowboy during the final days of the traditional American frontier? I could steal, kill, rob, and fight my way through situations like no tomorrow, at a detriment to my honor, of course. I could become the cowboy I always wanted to be. Through exploration, I also got to know Arthur for all his faults, likes, and dislikes. I learned of his loyalty, his love for a certain Mary Linton, and documentation of the world around him through his journals. Who I became while I explored was much different from the person I had to inhabit while taking on story missions. I became restricted by combat options, forced to inhabit an Arthur that was not my own.

Decisions weren't mine to make, and my worldview was stunted. While I was interested in seeing what happened next, the story worked against its exploration to become something more restrictive. While you don't have to see the story through or even participate in some of the story missions, there are specific missions that are a must-play because they unlock specific features, areas, or chapters. Players are made to take actions that affect overall honor, something that I took quite seriously during my first playthrough. I was invested in the world and the story, but I was forced to choose between seeing the story through my own eyes via exploration or through a curated mission, which sometimes left me with more questions than answers.

If I wanted to see the world Rockstar devs created on my own terms, I would potentially miss out on story missions that gave me more context about the characters I had come to love. One of my absolute favorite story missions that I almost completely missed upon my first playthrough was "We Love Once and True." The three-part optional quest is done for Mary Linton, where you help rescue her brother Jamie from a cult. Arthur and Mary's storyline is one of the most important in my book. Arthur's relationship with Mary contextualizes his internal struggles in choosing this life, as seen throughout, but mainly towards the end of the game.

My first playthrough was strictly about finding out how this story unravels, which meant I missed out on a ton. I felt roped into the story, which is a credit to the writers at Rockstar, but I also had no chance to catch my breath and just be.

Arthur is stuck choosing between himself and a happy life with Mary or the life Dutch Van der Linde wants for him. His relationship with Mary is emphasized in this optional story mission. If I missed it, I would be foregoing key characterization, but I would also maybe have understood other facets of the game through my exploration sans this mission. The story is amazing, and story missions bring context to Arthur's world, but so does exploration. Blocking sightseeing and discovery with story missions is a double-edged sword that Rockstar has trouble getting right, even in their many GTA titles.

Red Dead Online Is a Start, but Not Nearly Enough

Red Dead Online is a start, as far as balancing both story and exploration goes. While it isn't the focal point, there is a story for RD Online , although it has nothing to do with the main story featured in RDR2 's dedicated story mode. Players pilot a silent custom protagonist who is freed from prison after being framed for a murder. Players must work alongside a woman named Jessica LeClerk to clear their name and get revenge on the people who killed her husband. There is still a dedicated honor system and missions to complete tied to this side story, but exploration is not hindered by it.

If I wanted to see the world Rockstar devs created on my own terms, I would potentially miss out on story missions that gave me more context about the characters I had come to love.

Online is true to that Wild West feel. It's anyone's game. Players can virtually do just about anything and everything they want. Players can pursue different roles like Bounty Hunter or Collector, they can play in groups for a unique experience, and they can create their own character that feels more like themselves than Arthur. In short, players have more control over their destinies and can explore as they want. That being said, Rockstar's RD Online build is infamously unfinished, meaning the story ends on a cliffhanger and the world is less reactive to a player, which is something that I really loved in story mode. Story mode is extremely detailed, which is why it is a shame that most players miss out on hidden details because they are so tied to story missions that make exploration more challenging.

Story mode is a must-play, especially for first-timers. That being said, exploration can be limited by that wonderful storytelling. It's hard to choose what to go for, especially since the world Rockstar built is so appealing. For that reason, story mode missions can be somewhat restrictive, while RD Online features more balance between story and exploration. While it is nearly there, RD Online 's world and story need to be more like the expansive story mode build. More in-depth, with more reactive moments like deep NPC dialogue and little environmental tidbits that keep me on my toes. I want to digest the world around me just as much as I want to understand an amazing story.

It's thanks to the exceptional story and characters that Red Dead Redemption 2 has the longevity that it does. Rockstar Games created a generational narrative with just about anything a person could want from a good story, from love and longing to murder and governmental interference. Characters are tangible beings with wants and desires that manifest in actions, whether good or evil, that change the course of the story. That impeccable writing is what keeps me coming back to RDR2 again and again.

Sure, I have a ton of games on my list that I need to play, but I also want to keep riding and bonding with my horse, talking to members of the Van der Linde gang, and chatting with wonderful and weird NPCs in RDR2 . Story mode is a joy to run through again and again, but the story missions can sometimes stunt exploration for players, playing out scenarios strictly without the player's control. These story missions inadvertently set invisible boundaries that keep players from inhabiting the world Rockstar built to its fullest. With strict boundaries in mind, how are players meant to get the most out of the thoughtfully crafted world and story?
